newsitem.title: USA: Boeing chair sees airlines bearing costs.
newsitem.headline: Boeing chair sees airlines bearing costs.

text.p: Boeing Co Chairman Frank Shrontz said Tuesday he expected airlines to bear most costs of any changes ordered for the company's jets by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration.

The National Transportation Safety Board staff is considering several proposed changes to Boeing 737 jets and other models including the installation of devices to prevent sudden uncommanded rudder movements.
Such movements are suspected in two unsolved 737 crashes including a 1994 Pittsburgh incident that killed all 132 on board.
Shrontz, who plans to retire as chairman around the end of the year, said he did not know what the recommendations would cost if adopted by the Federal Aviation Administration.
"I don't know what the cost impact is," Shrontz told reporters after a speech to Pacific Rim business leaders. "I would think the airlines would bear most of that."
On a separate issue, Shrontz said Russia had agreed to waive stiff tariffs to facilitate the planned purchase by flag carrier Aeroflot of 10 Boeing 737-400s.

He said the move spurred Boeing's decision to withdraw opposition to Aeroflot's purchase of 20 Russian IL-96 planes powered by United Technologies Corp Pratt & Whitney engines and financed by the U.S. Export-Import Bank.
Boeing chief financial officer Boyd Givan told Reuters the Pratt & Whitney deal would have to close before he would know whether the Export-Import Bank also would finance the Boeing jets.
Shrontz also told reporters Boeing might not launch its planned 747 "stretch" jumbo jet until next year.
"I think it's possible it will go into next year," he said. "We've got to get significant numbers of orders from a couple or three very important customers."
British Airways Plc and Singapore Airlines Ltd have been the most vocal about the need for a jet larger than the 747.
